item.title: Kimberly Guilfoyle Resigns as Ambassador to Greece
item.description:
Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned as the U.S. ambassador to Greece on Tuesday after the White House asked her to do so following a string of damaging reports, including that she had asked a Republican donor to pay off her credit card.

In response to a question from a reporter about Ms. Guilfoyle’s status, President Trump’s new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, said: “We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign. She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well.”

Mr. Trump said Tuesday that Ms. Guilfoyle “was doing a good job” but that he “didn’t like what I read.” The president also downplayed his connection to Ms. Guilfoyle, who was once engaged to his oldest son, Donald Trump Jr.

“She wasn’t a member of my family,” he told reporters before leaving the White House for Alaska. “She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago.”

In a lengthy post on social media, Ms. Guilfoyle said that her time as ambassador was “coming to an end” and that she planned to “vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.”

“I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service,” she wrote.

A donor, Eric Deters, first told The Wall Street Journal that Ms. Guilfoyle asked him to wire her $100,000 to pay off her American Express card just before her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025. According to messages Mr. Deters provided to The New York Times, Ms. Guilfoyle promised to serve as his “ride or die in Trump world” if he sent her the money.

Ms. Guilfoyle was one of the first ambassadors to be nominated in the president’s second term. In Greece, she has been a highly visible ambassador, appearing on the cover of Vogue Greece and at parties around Athens. Ms. Guilfoyle told The Times last year that her active social life demonstrated her commitment to the job.

In her resignation post, Ms. Guilfoyle said she was proud of her work to expand American liquefied natural gas exports to Europe and strengthen defense and security partnerships with NATO.

In Athens, the reports of her potential conflicts of interest have generated exasperation.

“The fact that they would send someone like that here, with no tact or diplomacy skills, shows how low we rank in Trump’s priorities, how insignificant Greece is for them,” Maria Stefanou, a 68-year-old retiree, told The Times last week.

Greece’s foreign ministry declined to comment, but opposition parties said the reports that had led to Ms. Guilfoyle’s resignation raised important questions about foreign interference in Greek politics and the country’s business interests.

“The decision to remove the ambassador implicitly lends credence to these reports, which in essence confirm a model of transactional diplomacy, far removed from the principled foreign policy that Greece should be pursuing,” Dimitris Mantzos, a spokesman for Pasok, the main center-left opposition party, wrote in a statement.

Mr. Mantzos said his party had asked for details about the energy and defense agreements signed last week during Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to Athens.

Ms. Guilfoyle welcomed Mr. Rubio upon his arrival, and the two spent much of the trip together, as is customary when a top official travels overseas. When asked about the reports, Mr. Rubio defended Ms. Guilfoyle and said she “has been a strong ambassador.” But when the Journal article with Mr. Deters’s allegations published shortly before Mr. Rubio departed Greece, he brushed aside questions about the matter, saying, “I’m not going to comment on a story that literally posted a few hours ago.”

The resignation caps a remarkable rise and fall for Ms. Guilfoyle, a former Fox News personality. Decades ago, she was married to Gavin Newsom, then the mayor of San Francisco, and in 2004, Harper’s Bazaar predicted their marriage would be “one of the most glamorous political unions since Jack and Jackie.” They divorced in 2006.

Ms. Guilfoyle then became a legal analyst for CNN and ABC before joining Fox News. She was forced out of Fox in 2018 over questions about inappropriate workplace behavior. That same year, she started dating Donald Trump Jr. and working for a pro-Trump super PAC. The two were engaged in 2020, and Ms. Guilfoyle spoke at both the 2020 and 2024 Republican National Conventions. In May, the president’s son married Bettina Anderson, a Palm Beach socialite.

“While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end,” Ms. Guilfoyle wrote on social media.

Niki Kitsantonis and Edward Wong contributed reporting from Athens.

item.title: Miami Tugboat Captain Gets 18 Months in Crash That Killed 3 Children
item.description:
The captain of a 25-foot tugboat pushing a barge that struck a sailboat off Miami Beach last year, killing three children from a sailing camp, was sentenced to 18 months in prison on Tuesday, his lawyer said.

The captain, Yusiel Lopez Insua, 47, of Miami, pleaded guilty in July to a count of seaman’s manslaughter in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida.

Judge Jacqueline Becerra went above the sentence recommended by the prosecution and Mr. Insua’s lawyer. Under the plea agreement, they proposed a sentence of 12 months and one day in prison, to be followed by six months of home detention. He had faced up to 10 years in prison, prosecutors said.

His lawyer, Walter A. Reynoso, said in a statement on Tuesday that he “respects and accepts the 18-month sentence imposed by the Honorable Judge Becerra.”

Mr. Reynoso added, “Yusiel is profoundly sorry, and accepted responsibility for his conduct that caused this heart-wrenching, life-altering tragedy.”

At the sentencing hearing, the judge compared what Mr. Insua did to driving down Interstate 95 blindfolded, according to WSVN-TV Channel 7.

The U.S. Coast Guard received a report just before 11:30 a.m. on July 28, 2025, that a barge had hit a sailboat near Hibiscus Island and Monument Island in Miami Beach.

Mr. Insua was using the tugboat to push the barge across Biscayne Bay when the craft slammed into a stalled sailboat, which was carrying five girls, ages 7 to 13, and a 19-year-old camp counselor, prosecutors said. The Miami Yacht Club said that the children and the counselor were taking part in a sailing camp run by the Miami Youth Sailing Foundation.

The counselor and two of the children survived after being dragged beneath the barge. Three of the girls were killed in the collision.

The Miami-Dade County Medical Examiner’s Office identified two of the victims as Mila Yankelevich, 7, and Erin Ko, 13. Days later, the family of a third victim, Arielle Buchman, 10, announced that she, too, had died.

The camp counselor had tried to warn Mr. Insua of the sailboat’s presence, prosecutors said, but his forward view was obstructed and no one had been assigned as a lookout.

Mr. Insua failed to see the stalled sailboat before the barge ran over it, submerging it beneath the hull, prosecutors said.

A forensic analysis of Mr. Insua’s phone found evidence of internet activity around the time of the collision, according to prosecutors.

Mr. Insua was set to be placed under house arrest for the next 60 days and then surrender himself to the authorities in December, according to WSVN.

Michael Levenson contributed reporting.

item.title: Texas Prosecutors May Seek Charges Against ICE Agent Who Hit Fleeing Man
item.description:
Texas prosecutors are considering criminal charges against an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who struck and injured a Mexican construction worker with a vehicle in Houston over the weekend, officials said.

The worker, Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, an undocumented immigrant, was driving to his job on Saturday morning when federal immigration authorities tried to pull him over in unmarked vehicles, according to Cesar Espinosa, the executive director of FIEL, an immigrant rights group assisting Mr. Parra Hernandez’s family.

When Mr. Parra Hernandez stopped the car, he and a passenger tried to flee. ICE said in a statement on Saturday that Mr. Parra Hernandez had run in front of one of the agency’s vehicles and was struck. But surveillance footage from a nearby business captured Mr. Parra Hernandez and another man running away as an ICE vehicle veered around the corner and appeared to hit Mr. Parra Hernandez from behind.

He remained hospitalized on Tuesday and will have to undergo multiple surgeries, Mr. Espinosa said. One of his legs was broken, Mr. Espinosa added, and he suffered injuries to his hips and an ankle.

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Tuesday.

Sean Teare, the district attorney in Harris County, which includes Houston, said investigators from his office were looking into the incident as a possible aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. He said investigators also believed that the vehicle that struck Mr. Parra Hernandez was carrying people detained from an earlier incident and that the driver should not have been pursuing the construction worker.

Mr. Teare said that federal agents removed the ICE vehicle from the scene contrary to standard investigation protocol and over the objections of local investigators.

“That is just not the way that law enforcement behaves,” Mr. Teare said in an interview. “Every step of the way, the behavior of these agents, and of ICE as a whole, on our streets is certainly not best practice. It is making every person in our community less safe.”

ICE has faced scrutiny from state and local officials over traffic stops, which have been central to the Trump administration’s escalation of immigration arrests this summer and have at times turned deadly.

Local officials and immigrant rights groups in Houston said residents were still shaken over the July killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a father and owner of a construction business who had also been on his way to work when he was followed by unmarked ICE vehicles.

In both cases, ICE said its officers were searching for a different person. In its statement on Saturday, ICE said that agents were trying to arrest Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, a Mexican immigrant with a deportation order and prior arrests for driving under the influence and the unlawful possession of a firearm.

ICE said that agents spotted him climbing into Mr. Parra Hernandez’s vehicle before they tried to stop the vehicle. Mr. Mendoza-Cervantes has not been found, the agency said.

Kim Bruno, Mr. Parra Hernandez’s lawyer, and Mr. Espinosa said that Mr. Parra Hernandez and other witnesses disputed that account, arguing that Mr. Mendoza-Cervantes was not in the vehicle and that Mr. Parra Hernandez did not know him.

Investigators with the Harris County District Attorney’s Office are now contacting residents and nearby businesses for additional witness testimony and surveillance footage.

Rodolfo Parra, 34, Mr. Parra Hernandez’s brother, said his family wanted justice for Mr. Parra Hernandez. The family believed he was dead until a friend helped find him at a hospital, the brother said.

Mr. Parra Hernandez, a native of the Mexican state of Puebla, has lived in Houston since he first made his way to the United States as a teenager in the early 1990s, his brother said. He had not been stopped by immigration authorities before and had no criminal record, his relatives and immigration lawyer said.

Mr. Parra, the brother, said he and his family had watched the news reports about Mr. Salgado Araujo with sadness. “We never thought we would be in a similar situation,” he said. “We don’t wish this on anyone.”

item.title: U.A.W. Re-elects Shawn Fain as President
item.description:
Shawn Fain was re-elected to a second term as president of the United Auto Workers, despite allegations of misconduct that threatened to overshadow his national political stature and his successes at the helm of the union.

Mr. Fain, a profane and combative leader, prevailed over a divided field that included former allies who split with him, and who have publicly criticized his tactics to expand the union’s numbers and influence.

The U.S. attorney’s office in Detroit has opened a criminal investigation into Mr. Fain’s conduct, prompted by a federal monitor’s findings that he had abused his authority. It is not clear how the union would respond if he were indicted.

Mr. Fain said the results demonstrated that U.A.W. members “are united and want us to keep fighting and building on what we’ve done.”

“These results are about taking on corporate America and reversing the worst out-of-control wealth inequality in America’s history,” he said in a statement. “We are fighting for the entire working class, whether that’s at the bargaining table, organizing new members, or in the political arena.”

The unofficial vote count was released on Tuesday in a report filed in federal court by the monitor, who oversees the union’s elections as part of a 2021 court settlement to resolve corruption charges involving some of Mr. Fain’s predecessors.

According to the monitor’s report, Mr. Fain received about two-thirds of the votes cast. The union has about 400,000 active members, and roughly 100,000 ballots were accepted.

Mr. Fain was elected in 2023 as a reformer. But he has been at odds with the monitor, starting with a series of tense exchanges in the wake of the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks in Israel.

In recent months, Mr. Fain has accused Neil Barofsky, the federal monitor, of targeting him over his political stances, in particular the union’s support for a cease-fire in Gaza. Mr. Barofsky has accused Mr. Fain of abusing his authority and retaliating against board members who refused to do his bidding.

Both men have denied wrongdoing. Federal prosecutors in Detroit, who are participating in oversight of the union, opened a grand jury investigation into Mr. Fain prompted by the monitor’s findings.

A representative for the U.S. attorney’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Fain rose to prominence in 2024 when the U.A.W. staged a strike against General Motors, Ford Motor and Stellantis, winning substantial raises — contracts set to expire in May 2028. Other negotiations are coming up in 2027, including at General Dynamics Land Systems and John Deere.

item.title: Katie Zacharia Stepped to the Lectern for the First Time. It Was a Bumpy Ride.
item.description:
President Trump’s new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, made her debut behind the White House lectern Tuesday morning.

It was a bumpy one.

“Good morning!” she began. “I want to thank President Trump for his trust that he has placed in me. I have wanted to work for him for a very long time.”

She spent the next eight minutes reading nervously from a script, looking up at the cameras every couple of lines. Then she said she was ready to take some questions. She called on only three reporters, dropped one wild piece of news, made a slip mixing up her husband and her president, then darted out of there after just five and a half minutes, leaving the White House press corps to scratch its collective head.

All told, Ms. Zacharia picked only a few outlets from a list she was holding: Breitbart, Fox News and The Daily Mail.

The White House press secretary gig is a tricky one that, when practiced well, involves more than reciting talking points on cable TV, which is what Ms. Zacharia was doing as a commentator on Fox News when she got picked for this job. Of the few questions she allowed on Tuesday, the most substantive one was also among the most predictable: “Has the U.S. stopped sharing intel with Ukraine?”

For days, the breakdown of U.S. negotiations with the Ukrainians has been front page news — certainly it is the dominant story line in Washington this week — and yet, Ms. Zacharia was not prepared to answer the question.

“I’ll have to get back to you on that,” she said.

One of the few questions she took was about how she hoped to “manage” her new job with a husband and four kids at home (hard to imagine a male press secretary getting that one). There was a moment of levity in the room when she caught herself in a funny slip, and was able to laugh about it. “So, my president, excuse me, my husband,” she said, “that’s a good one.”

She did come armed with one special surprise to drop. When a reporter asked about the fate of the U.S. Ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, Ms. Zacharia said, “We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign.”

Reporters in the room lit up — News!!! — but before they could ask more about this development, the new press secretary announced that she was ready to “end it,” because it was nearly time for the president’s departure. Reporters pelted questions at her as she prepared to edge out of the room toward the little sliding door painted blue.

“Can you take a few more questions?”

“Just a few more!”

“Did the president speak with Ambassador Guilfoyle?”

“What about the Russian diesel! Will the diesel come into the States?!”

Having not yet mastered the hard exit, she replied, “He will answer those questions out at Marine One.”

In the history of White House press secretaries, the ones who tend to do best have direct access to the president and therefore feel comfortable speaking on his behalf. Those who don’t end up having trouble in the job. Under President George W. Bush, that was Scott McClellan. Karine Jean-Pierre, the press secretary under President Joseph R. Biden Jr., did not often give the impression that she had been in the room with her boss.

Karoline Leavitt, Ms. Zacharia’s predecessor, really was part of Mr. Trump’s inner circle, and because she was with him on the campaign trail when he was mounting his comeback, she could speak for him with some authority. Ms. Zacharia, 41, is not only new to the president but also to a lot of the people who work for him in the White House.

At 27, Ms. Leavitt was the youngest person ever to hold the job. Behind the podium, she could be lacerating, vitriolic, dissembling. But she didn’t seem scared, exactly.

Reporters are animals. They can smell fear. Ms. Leavitt used to post photos of herself on Instagram sparring with a packed briefing room set to the soundtrack of “Welcome to the Jungle” by Guns N’ Roses.

Welcome to the jungle, it gets worse here every day.You learn to live like an animal, in the jungle where we play.

Not long after the briefing, Ms. Zacharia walked out of the White House with the president onto the South Lawn, where a massive, gnashing press maw was waiting. Ms. Zacharia stood off to the side while her boss prowled the pavement, fielding questions about Iran and Ukraine and the midterms and the end of Ms. Guilfoyle’s chapter as Our Woman in Athens.

The president was asked how he thought Ms. Zacharia had fared in her first briefing, and why she had taken so few questions.

“I thought she was very good,” he said.

In the social media post he made last week announcing her appointment, he called her “an attorney,” and she identifies herself as a lawyer. This reporter asked the president in which state Ms. Zacharia had passed the bar exam. Mr. Trump turned to look at his new press secretary. She took two small steps closer. “When I moved to China,” she said.

Asked later for clarification, White House officials would not say whether or where Ms. Zacharia passed a bar exam.

Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, provided this statement over email: “Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team. She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as press secretary.”

Mr. Trump finished taking questions, turned and traipsed toward his helicopter. Ms. Zacharia was left standing alone. The reporters began shouting in her direction.

“Katie! Katie!”

They waved her over. She just smiled and stared straight ahead.

After another moment, the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles, appeared with two of the president’s most trusted aides, Natalie Harp and Walt Nauta. Ms. Zacharia joined her new co-workers and together they all walked silently across the South Lawn and climbed into Marine One to begin a long day of travel to Alaska followed by Las Vegas.

Plenty of time for everybody to get to know each other a little better.

]]>

item.title: Justice Dept. Issues Subpoenas in Ilhan Omar Investigation
item.description:
Federal agents investigating Representative Ilhan Omar, Democrat of Minnesota, have issued subpoenas to some relatives as officials scour her family’s history for evidence of fraud and false statements in immigration paperwork, according to people familiar with the matter.

A sister of Ms. Omar’s, Sahra Noor, received a subpoena, as did at least one other member of her family circle, according to people familiar with the investigation. On Monday, D.H.S. agents executed a search warrant at her home in Washington, carrying out boxes of documents, the people said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss investigative steps.

Ms. Noor, a health care professional and author, did not reply to requests for comment sent by email and made in a call with someone who identified herself as a daughter of Ms. Noor’s.

Grand jury subpoenas are issued to gather evidence about possible crimes, and do not mean that the recipients themselves are under investigation. On Monday, Ms. Omar condemned the search of her home, calling it an effort by the Trump administration “to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” She has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing on immigration matters.

The specifics of the investigation into Ms. Omar remain unclear, but in recent months, federal investigators have been scrutinizing her family’s immigration history. The inquiry focuses in part on whether Ms. Omar’s late father, Nur Omar Mohamed, lied or omitted information in immigration forms before becoming a U.S. citizen.

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

The subpoenas are another investigative step the Justice Department is taking just a few weeks before Election Day, a time when law enforcement officials typically avoid taking overt measures, such as executing search warrants and issuing subpoenas, that could be seen as trying to help or hurt a candidate. Prosecutors have sometimes been willing to carry out such steps if they have reason to believe evidence could be destroyed, or if other crimes could be committed.

Such steps so close to the election, on the heels of President Trump’s public attacks on Ms. Omar, have raised questions about how much of the case is based on political pressure from the White House, and how much of it is based on solid evidence. In his second term, the president has publicly demanded that the Justice Department charge certain people with crimes, and has at times fired those who declined to do so.

The president on Tuesday suggested on social media that Ms. Omar had engaged in fraud to make millions of dollars. He also suggested she had engaged in immigration fraud. “America wants answers, and we want them, NOW!” he said.

Randall D. Eliason, a former federal prosecutor and retired law professor, said that the Trump Justice Department had so eroded trust that it had “sort of forfeited the right to a presumption of regularity,” a legal term for federal judges assuming prosecutors are acting in good faith.

“With all of the other things they have done to politicize the department and use its power to go after the president’s enemies,” he continued, “it certainly looks extremely suspicious. But without seeing the search warrant affidavit, you can’t say for certain.”

Norman L. Eisen, a lawyer who has repeatedly sued the Trump administration in recent months, announced on social media on Tuesday that a nonprofit group he works for had requested an investigation into whether administration officials violated the Hatch Act by “orchestrating” the search of Ms. Omar’s home. The request was made to the Office of the Special Counsel, which oversees enforcement of the Hatch Act, a law that puts limits on the political activities of federal employees.

“Officials can’t use criminal power to affect an election,” Mr. Eisen wrote. “This is the textbook case.”

Ms. Omar has represented a solidly blue district that includes Minneapolis since 2019. She won her primary election in a landslide earlier this year and does not face a competitive Republican rival on the November ballot.

Ms. Omar’s immigration history has been investigated by federal authorities for over a decade, but those inquiries have not led to charges. In an interview in March, Vice President JD Vance declared that Ms. Omar was “definitely guilty” of immigration fraud.

At a political rally on Saturday, two days before the search, Mr. Trump singled out Ms. Omar and her Somali heritage, and mentioned Mr. Vance’s efforts overseeing fraud investigations. “Let’s see what happens,” he said.

On Tuesday, Mr. Vance said he did not have any advance knowledge of the search of Ms. Omar’s home.

“The president and I largely try to stay out of Department of Justice investigations and other prosecutions,” Mr. Vance said, adding: “If there’s a real case there, we’re going to follow the facts. If there’s not a real case there, then we won’t.”

]]>

item.title: Elon Musk Re-Enters the Chat
item.description:
For Republicans, Christmas came in July.

That’s when Elon Musk began funneling more than $276 million into the party’s efforts to save its majorities in Congress, my colleague Teddy Schleifer has learned.

It is a stonkingly large amount of money, and it includes, in sum, one of the biggest political donations in history: $158 million to Senate Republicans’ main super PAC, the Senate Leadership Fund.

It means that when we talk about the Republicans’ considerable outside spending advantage over Democrats in this midterm, we are talking, in large part, about Musk’s personal contributions.

And it means that a mercurial figure who once backed off political spending is back in the game.

Musk, of course, spent big on President Trump’s 2024 campaign, then joined his administration for a short-lived stint as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency. He poured cash into a Supreme Court race in Wisconsin, only for his preferred candidate to lose. A few months into Trump’s term, he was publicly feuding with the president over the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and promising to start his own third party.

I asked Teddy to join us to explain why Musk — who has been popping up by Trump’s side more frequently in recent weeks — is making his way back into politics, and how his money is shaping Republicans’ campaign strategy.

Jess: Teddy, I’m old enough to remember when, in 2025, Elon Musk said he was going to do “a lot less” political spending. Turns out he’s already spent more on the midterms than he did on the whole 2024 presidential election. Why did he change his mind?

Teddy: If you are willing to ignore a three-month anti-Trump bender from Musk in mid-2025, he’s actually been rather consistent. Toward the end of his time overseeing the Department of Government Efficiency, Musk obviously got rather nihilistic about politics and the Trump movement. But the September 2025 killing of Charlie Kirk affected him, I’ve been told, and made him angry at the left. And by November, I reported that he and Trump were largely peachy again. (Not that he ever retracted his desire to start a third party.)

He is back to where he was in 2024 — genuinely fearful of what happens to his vision of America if Democrats win. But it’s not just that Musk is a true believer. I also think Musk knows that there is a real business risk to Democrats winning in November. There could be congressional investigations into DOGE, and maybe his companies.

Is that what’s personally at stake for Musk in the midterms? Concerns about oversight?

That’s part of it. Musk is also likely to be a donor in 2028 — we report in the story that his own super PAC, America PAC, plans to spend in the next cycle — and I think he wants it known just how much he’s doing to help the party.

I also think that Musk is driven a lot by what he sees online. The Texas Senate race, which he has shown a particular interest in, is viral in a way that no other race is. He is a human being, surrounded by right-wing friends in Texas and, more importantly, inundated with digital stimuli about James Talarico, Ken Paxton and that dynamic race.

How does Musk’s spending fit into the Republican midterm strategy, more broadly?

One question I’ve had for weeks is about the provenance of the $158 million that the outside Senate Republican group is spending to help Paxton in Texas. How exactly did the Senate Leadership Fund “come up” with this money? Well, I learned as part of my reporting that this decision in late August by the super PAC was preceded by Musk sending a total of $158 million their way. That, uh, helps.

Plus it wasn’t totally clear to me, when I began calling around, how America PAC precisely fit into the Republican operation. One revelation for me was that Musk was asked by Trump’s aides to reprise his super PAC field program from 2024, and I know that Musk’s team is on regular conference calls with the Trump team and entities like S.L.F. The Trump team is counting on the Musk operation and its thousands of canvassers.

In 2025, we saw Musk standing onstage in Green Bay in a cheesehead, attempting to amp up Republicans in a Wisconsin Supreme Court race they ultimately lost by 10 percentage points. Is he taking the show on the road this year?

I think that Wisconsin loss was embarrassing for Musk and actually cast a long shadow, explaining a lot about what happened next. Musk appeared aware in private conversations after that defeat that he could be a bit of a liability to the causes he cared about, and I don’t think it’s a surprise that he is playing things much more quietly this time around.

It’s also true, based on my sources, that Musk just isn’t preoccupied with these midterms. He himself isn’t involved in day-to-day operations as he was last time. His friends tell me he isn’t paying much attention to the midterms at all. And Jess, his own X feed tells you all you need to know: He is rarely tweeting about any specific candidates, outside of Talarico. And even those are relatively rare. This ain’t 2024, or even 2025!

Get Caught Up

Under pressure from the White House, Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned as U.S. ambassador to Greece. The Wall Street Journal reported last week that Guilfoyle had asked a Republican donor to pay off $100,000 on her American Express credit card.

Trump denied that he was close with Guilfoyle, who used to be engaged to Donald Trump Jr. “She wasn’t a member of my family,” the president said today. “She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago.”

Trump described his new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as an attorney. But when a Times reporter asked today where she had passed the bar, she responded, “When I moved to China.” It’s not clear what she meant.

Trump is going to Alaska this evening to rally for Senator Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent. Vice President JD Vance went there last week, too, as Republicans try to hold on to the closely contested seat.

Top Republican super PACs are cutting off financial support for two House members: Tom Kean Jr. in New Jersey and Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa. It’s the first instance this cycle of Republican groups abandoning incumbents.

Debate season rages on. There are debates tonight for the Senate races in Maine, Georgia and Iowa. We’ll have the highlights in tomorrow’s newsletter.

Quote of the Day

That was Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, talking about A.I.

El-Sayed released a platform on how he would handle the technology. His proposals include the creation of a cabinet-level agency to regulate the technology and a ban on recursive self-improvement (i.e., using A.I. to create ever-more-advanced A.I. models).

Chart of the Day

Who won last week’s Michigan Senate debate? Your answer might depend on what side of social media you were watching.

Using more than 13,000 X posts from both sides of the political spectrum, Stuart Thompson reconstructed how the left and the right tried to shape the narrative of the night.

Mailbag

Readers recently wrote in to The Morning, The Times’s daily news briefing, with their burning political questions, and our reporters provided answers. Here’s one.

Will ICE agents be at polling places? — Robert Halper, West Orange, N.J.

Alexandra Berzon, an investigative reporter who writes about election systems, said:

Although some election officials and voting advocates worry that this prospect will drive away voters, they say the law is clear: Armed federal agents are not allowed in polling places. Administration officials have spread misinformation about the voter rolls, saying they bulge with noncitizens, but the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice have said there are no plans to deploy armed agents to patrol polling places. (Government lawyers, on the other hand, are often on site.)

You can read more questions and answers here.

In One Number

That’s the annual home insurance premium in Kansas for a $300,000 house with a $1,000 deductible. It’s 84 percent higher than the national average.

Many Americans’ home insurance costs have soared in recent years, driven up by wildfires, hurricanes, floods and tornadoes worsened by climate change. In an election cycle so focused on affordability, that rising price tag has helped push reliably red states like Kansas and Florida onto the battlefield.

One Last Thing

A Republican super PAC trying to boost Senator Susan Collins in her tough re-election fight in Maine spent thousands of dollars to run an attack ad against her challenger, Troy Jackson, in Portland.

It’s not likely to have much of an effect. That’s because the ad was shown to more than a million viewers in Oregon — home to the other Portland.

The vendor responsible for buying the ads took the blame for the blunder and said it was refunding the super PAC. Still, Jackson’s campaign pounced, saying Collins and her allies “are so out of touch with Maine, they apparently can’t find it on a map.”

Taylor Robinson contributed to this newsletter.

]]>

item.title: 5 Takeaways From a Heated and Personal Maine Senate Debate
item.description:
Senator Susan Collins of Maine, a vulnerable Republican, and Troy Jackson, her Democratic challenger, sparred on Tuesday over health care, the war in Iran and the senator’s record in a policy-heavy and sometimes tense debate.

The showdown, held at a TV studio in Bangor, was the third of four scheduled debates in a hotly contested race that could be critical to determining which party controls the Senate.

Here are five takeaways from the hourlong debate.

The debate closed with an exchange that distilled one of the overarching disputes in the race.

Throughout the debate, Ms. Collins, who is chair of the influential Appropriations Committee, highlighted areas where she said she had used her power to deliver for Maine, securing benefits for Mainers even in legislation she ultimately opposed.

Mr. Jackson argued in his closing remarks that she had instead used her power to enable President Trump.

“Tonight I believe you heard two very different ideas of what a senator owes the people of Maine,” Mr. Jackson said. “Senator Collins wants credit for her power. I believe you have to be responsible for what you do with it.”

Ms. Collins, in her own closing remarks, suggested that Mr. Jackson would lack her ability to deliver for the state — saying he “struggled to get his bills passed” as a state lawmaker.

“When you live in a small state like Maine, who you send to Washington really matters,” Ms. Collins said. “I have proven time and time again that I deliver.”

At one point, the debate turned tense and personal.

When Ms. Collins said she was concerned about fraud in Medicare and Medicaid programs, Mr. Jackson pointed to a report that the F.B.I. last year shut down an inquiry into corruption allegations against a political adviser to Ms. Collins.

“I am shocked that you are talking about fraud because there’s only one person up here that’s been accused of that by the F.B.I.,” Mr. Jackson said.

Ms. Collins has not been accused of fraud by the F.B.I. Last month, ProPublica reported that the agency had looked into Ms. Collins’s interactions with a donor seeking federal contracts. The inquiry was closed under the Trump administration.

The senator bristled at Mr. Jackson’s assertion.

“Troy has repeatedly insulted my integrity all evening long,” Ms. Collins said, adding, “He lied when he said that I was under investigation and found to have committed fraud by the F.B.I.”

Mr. Jackson replied, “I didn’t say that she was guilty; I said that they were investigating.”

Mr. Jackson said Ms. Collins was to blame for the war in Iran, which has caused a surge in energy prices.

Ms. Collins said that she was aligned with Democrats on the war, and that the president had erred in his execution of the conflict.

“Troy and I agree that the war should come to end,” said Ms. Collins, who has voted against the war since April, after initially supporting it.

She added: “I agree that the president did not have a good plan. He should have anticipated the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.”

Ms. Collins noted that there were not enough votes in Congress to force the president to withdraw from the conflict.

“Senator Susan Collins says that she voted against it nine times, but she didn’t have the votes,” Mr. Jackson said. “Well that sounds like then we probably ought to have Democrats in charge of the U.S. Senate so that we have the votes.”

From the start of the debate, Mr. Jackson blamed Ms. Collins for a surge in fuel oil costs caused by the war in Iran — an issue that is hitting hard in Maine, where half the homes are warmed with heating oil.

“I would get us out of the Iran war, unlike Senator Collins,” Jackson said, declaring that the senator “does whatever Donald Trump wants.”

Ms. Collins emphasized that she had helped expedite the release of federal heating assistance for lower-income Maine residents.

Mr. Jackson dismissed the move as a “short-term Band-Aid” for a challenge that would be “horrific for people in this state.”

“What about the back-end, when that money’s all spent?” Mr. Jackson said. “People are still going to be struggling to fill their oil tanks.

The debate included a granular discussion of health care, with Mr. Jackson claiming that Ms. Collins had supported cuts to health care funding in the president’s signature domestic policy law.

Ms. Collins, who helped enable the passage of the bill by voting yes on a procedural vote, noted that she had ultimately voted against it. She accused Mr. Jackson of misrepresenting her record. And she said she and Mr. Jackson were aligned in their opposition to the bill — but that she had been able to secure funding for rural health care in Maine in the law.

Mr. Jackson suggested Ms. Collins was twisting his words.

“I didn’t say that she voted for it,” Mr. Jackson said. “I said she advanced it.”

The discussion ultimately devolved into an argument about Mr. Jackson’s understanding of health care policy.

Ms. Collins said Mr. Jackson was “confusing the Medicaid program with the Medicare program.”

Mr. Jackson appeared to be offended.

“Senator Collins is not going to stand there and school me on what I know,” he replied.

item.title: Mike Collins Attacks Back: 7 Takeaways From the Second Senate Debate in Georgia
item.description:
Senator Jon Ossoff, the Democratic incumbent, and Representative Mike Collins, the Republican challenger, debated for the second and final time on Tuesday in the contest for a Georgia Senate seat.

Mr. Collins, who faced a barrage of attacks from Mr. Ossoff when the rivals debated last week, needed to find a way to make a final argument to independent voters. Georgians began voting early in person on Tuesday.

The congressman hit the senator harder than he did at the first debate, casting the election as a choice between “Georgia and Georgetown,” a reference to Mr. Ossoff’s alma mater. And the debate was somewhat less focused on the high costs that Mr. Ossoff has hammered Mr. Collins on throughout the campaign.

Here are seven takeaways from Tuesday night’s debate.

Polls suggest that Mr. Collins lags behind Mr. Ossoff in the race. Republicans have pulled some of their advertising money as a result, thinking it is better spent elsewhere before Nov. 3.

Perhaps sensing that his window to make an impression is closing, Mr. Collins tried to stick as much as he could on Mr. Ossoff. The congressman delivered his scripted opening more crisply than he did last week. Mr. Ossoff, Mr. Collins said, “views his success not as what he does for Georgia, but the number of clicks he gets on social media.”

Mr. Collins tried to hang inflation and ties to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein on Mr. Ossoff. He boasted about how Republicans limited illegal border crossings and painted Democrats, including Mr. Ossoff, as socialists.

Mr. Ossoff, for his part, continued to hound Mr. Collins on why he voted for higher tariffs, which have been blamed in part for rising prices. He also noted a House Ethics Committee review into allegations that Mr. Collins’s office had hired an intern who was romantically involved with the representative’s chief of staff and who had not performed any work. Mr. Collins dismissed the investigation as a “nothing burger.”

Mr. Collins could not avoid the steady stream of hits that continued from Mr. Ossoff on the congressman’s history of hiring aides who have espoused white nationalist and antisemitic views. At one point, a debate panelist asked Mr. Collins point blank if he was a white nationalist and what he wanted to say to “Black Georgians who question whether you will represent them equally.”

Mr. Collins answered “no,” seemingly to the question of whether he was a white nationalist, and said he condemned “any sort of hate speech, antisemitism, hate of any kind.”

J Street Action Fund, a liberal Jewish organization, has begun airing an anti-Collins digital ad noting those white nationalist ties. In both debates, Mr. Collins has tried to cast Ossoff, who is Jewish, as anti-Israel.

High diesel prices were the focus of much of the back-and-forth over the cost of living, with Mr. Ossoff pressing Mr. Collins to acknowledge the problem. Mr. Collins owns a trucking company in Jackson, Ga., his hometown.

“Diesel prices are high,” Mr. Collins conceded. But he maintained that more “supply is coming” and added that prices “will continue to come down.”

Mr. Ossoff’s campaign put out a video on Tuesday featuring a Georgia trucker, identified only as Richard, saying that he had voted for Mr. Trump three times but was backing “Senator Jon,” because “he’s listening to truck drivers like myself.”

Mr. Ossoff repeatedly pressed Mr. Collins to answer whether he still believed that Mr. Trump won the 2020 presidential election, a falsehood Mr. Collins has championed. Mr. Collins largely sidestepped the question. “Everybody’s seen my views on that,” he said at one point.

Georgia was the focal point for election denial in 2020, when Mr. Trump called the Republican secretary of state and asked him to “find” enough votes to reverse Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s victory.

On Tuesday, when Mr. Ossoff asked Mr. Collins to clarify, the congressman said: “There was a lot of doubt in that election. Yes, Joe Biden was the president. And yes, we saw the results of the Biden presidency.”

Mr. Ossoff, a canny user of social media, spread the term “Epstein class” earlier this year to refer to Mr. Trump and his big-donor allies. Mr. Epstein and his crimes have emerged as a major issue in this year’s midterm races.

On Tuesday, Mr. Collins reiterated his suggestion that Mr. Ossoff is a hypocrite for accepting campaign money from Reid Hoffman, the billionaire co-founder of LinkedIn who corresponded with Mr. Epstein and visited his island at least once. “This call is coming from inside the house,” Mr. Collins said.

Mr. Ossoff did not engage with the attack. Instead, he criticized Mr. Collins for voting against releasing the Epstein files until Mr. Trump agreed. “Who on your team advised you to raise the Epstein files?” Mr. Ossoff said. “You voted to cover up the evidence, Mike.”

Mr. Ossoff gave a shout-out to Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor who is the Democratic nominee for Georgia governor, saying it is “crucial” for Georgians to elect her because she wants to expand Medicaid in the state.

Mr. Ossoff made a similar pitch for Ms. Bottoms in last week’s debate as he tries to pull up down-ballot Democrats. Polls suggest that Ms. Bottoms is narrowly trailing the Republican nominee for governor, Rick Jackson, a wealthy health care executive.

The Democratic Governors Association announced on Tuesday that it was investing $10 million to help Ms. Bottoms in the race. Georgians have not elected a Democratic governor since 1998.

Mr. Ossoff has proved so adept at fund-raising and raising Democratic social media buzz that he has fielded questions for months about whether he might run for president in two years. He tried to put that chatter to rest once again in the answer to the debate’s very first question, when he was asked if he would commit to serving a full, six-year Senate term.

“Yes, I will,” Mr. Ossoff said. “I have zero interest in running for president. I’m not running for president. I’m running for re-election to the Senate.”
